body:
Ahmedabad: the ashram as a place for daily practice

Gandhi's first Indian ashram opened at Kochrab in Ahmedabad on 25 May 1915. It moved to the banks of the Sabarmati River on 17 June 1917. Ashram life provided a setting for spinning, other manual work and attempts to put collective discipline and social equality into practice. The ashram was therefore more than a residence: it connected constructive habits with the preparation of volunteers.

Kheda and Ahmedabad: different grievances in the same state

Both Kheda and Ahmedabad became important sites of Gandhi's early Indian campaigns in 1918. In Kheda, the issue was land revenue during crop distress; in Ahmedabad textile mills, it was workers' wages. Geography alone does not identify the grievance: an MCQ can pair the correct place with the wrong issue.

Gujarat Vidyapith: national education during Non-Cooperation

Gujarat Vidyapith was established in Ahmedabad on 18 October 1920 under Gandhi's guidance as a national educational institution and alternative to government-controlled education. Its approach connected learning with the mother tongue, productive work and social service. It also provides a Gujarat example of how the call to boycott colonial institutions was accompanied by efforts to establish Indian alternatives.

The institution's establishment in 1920 must not be confused with the later Wardha Basic Education proposals of 1937. The two belonged to the wider Gandhian concern with national education, but they were not the same event.

Sabarmati to Dandi: a Gujarat route with a national effect

The Salt March began at Sabarmati Ashram on 12 March 1930 and culminated in the breaking of the salt law at Dandi on 6 April 1930. Its starting place, destination and issue should be matched correctly: Sabarmati was the departure point, Dandi the coastal place where Gandhi defied the salt law.

Prelims focus

  • Kochrab Ashram: Ahmedabad, 25 May 1915.
  • Sabarmati Ashram: ashram moved to the river site on 17 June 1917.
  • Kheda and Ahmedabad: revenue relief and workers' wage dispute respectively, both in 1918.
  • Gujarat Vidyapith: 18 October 1920, Ahmedabad; national education.
  • Sabarmati–Dandi: 12 March–6 April 1930; protest against salt law.
  • Trap: Gujarat Vidyapith (1920) is not the Wardha Scheme (1937).

[Sources: Gandhi Heritage Portal, "Kochrab Ashram, Ahmedabad," site history; Sabarmati Ashram Preservation and Memorial Trust, "History of Gandhi Ashram at Sabarmati"; Gujarat Vidyapith, official "History" and "Journey," establishment dated 18 October 1920; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, ch. 9, printed pp. 115–122; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Gandhi chronology, 1930 entries (online sources consulted 21 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Gujarat supplied distinct examples of training, social work, education and public action.

title: The Gujarat Connection: Ashram Work, Public Protest and National Education

body:
Match the action before matching the date

An activity is best identified first by what participants actually did and which immediate problem it addressed. A shared broad aim—freedom from colonial rule—does not make every activity interchangeable. Use the following distinctions for factual, matching and short-statement questions.

ActivityImmediate purposeExample
Satyagraha through local protestResist a definite injustice without violence.Champaran: indigo grievances, 1917.
Non-cooperationWithdraw support from colonial goods or institutions.Foreign-cloth boycott, 1921.
Civil disobedienceDeliberately defy a specific unjust law.Salt law at Dandi, 1930.
KhadiSupport rural hand production and swadeshi.Charkha spinning and handloom weaving; AISA, 1925.
Other village industriesCreate local livelihoods and useful goods.Oil-pressing, soap-making and AIVIA, 1934.
Village sanitationImprove cleanliness of shared surroundings.Cleaning lanes, latrines and village wells.
Removal of untouchabilityEnd caste-based social exclusion.Equal access to wells and schools; Harijan Sevak Sangh, 1932.
Communal unityStrengthen cooperation among religious communities.Khilafat–Non-Cooperation cooperation, 1920–1921.
Basic educationConnect children's learning with productive work.Wardha education proposals, 1937.

Keep the constructive milestones in sequence

The major dates associated with educational institutions and constructive work are different from the dates of the national protests. The All-India Spinners' Association belongs to 1925, the Harijan Sevak Sangh to 1932, the All-India Village Industries Association to 1934 and the Wardha Basic Education proposals to 1937. The published presentation of Gandhi's constructive programme came later, in 1941, with a revised foreword dated 1945. These organisations and practices did not begin only when the book appeared.

Four frequent confusions

  • Kheda: peasants and land revenue; Ahmedabad: mill workers and wages.
  • Charkha: yarn; loom: cloth.
  • Sanitation: clean facility; anti-untouchability: equal access to facility.
  • Gujarat Vidyapith, 1920: national institution; Wardha, 1937: basic education proposals.

Prelims focus

  • Identify the immediate action and grievance before identifying the wider nationalist purpose.
  • Keep 1925 AISA, 1932 Harijan Sevak Sangh, 1934 AIVIA and 1937 Wardha in correct order.
  • Distinguish non-cooperation from civil disobedience by whether a specific law was openly broken.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, ch. 9, printed pp. 115–122; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, "Nationalism in India," secs. 1–3; NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class 11, ch. 3, printed pp. 31–38; M. K. Gandhi, Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place, "Foreword" and chapters 1–7; Gujarat Vidyapith, "History"; Gandhi Harijan Sevak Sangh, "History"; Mahatma Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialization, "Genesis of MGIRI"; Press Information Bureau, Wardha education feature (web sources consulted 21 November 2026).]
